title: Could Humans Evolve to Hold Their Breath Like Seals?
request: Biku's What's the Catch? what-if script, used as it is: 'Make a video on this script for the whats if part. make sure the animations are good like it should not be stuck in one photo for long time. each new info should bring a great animation' (2026-10-19).
sources: Ilardo, M. et al., "Physiological and genetic adaptations to diving in sea nomads", Cell, 2018. Bajau spleens about 50% larger than the neighbouring Saluan, also in Bajau who do not dive; a gene variant near PDE10A linked to spleen size. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.054

NPR (via KPBS), "The Secret To Deep Diving May Lie In The Spleen", 2018. Researchers still hope to confirm the thyroid hormone link and that red blood cell levels change during dives. https://www.kpbs.org/news/2018/04/24/the-secret-to-deep-diving-may-lie-in-the-spleen

AFP report on the Cell study (via Philstar), 2018. Bajau spend up to 60% of their working day diving. https://www.philstar.com/business/science-and-environment/2018/04/20/1807756/scientists-discover-secret-why-bajaus-are-stronger-divers

The Scientist, "Free Divers from Southeast Asia Evolved Bigger Spleens", 2018. A rare example of natural selection in modern humans, over hundreds to thousands of years. https://mobile.the-scientist.com/article/52347/free-divers-from-southeast-asia-evolved-bigger-spleens

Guinness World Records, "Longest time breath held voluntarily underwater (male)". 29 min 3 sec, Vitomir Maričić, Opatija, Croatia, 14 June 2025, after pre-breathing pure oxygen. https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/longest-time-breath-held-voluntarily-male

Checked by Claude on 2026-10-19 against Science News, NPR, The Scientist, Scientific American and reports of the record; no source gives the size of the spleens, so "roughly the size of a tennis ball" is unchecked.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Could your body ever evolve to hold its breath like a *seal*?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The surprise is that, somewhere on Earth, it has *already* happened.

shots.words: Could your body ever evolve to hold its breath like a *seal*?

overlay.text: Could Humans Evolve to Hold Their Breath Like Seals?

shots.words: The surprise is that, somewhere on Earth, it has *already* happened.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Most of us come up for air within about a minute, and think that is our *limit*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: But your body hides an old diving trick, and it starts in your *chest*.

shots.words: Most of us come up for air within about a minute, and think that is our *limit*.
But your body hides an old diving trick, and it starts in your *chest*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: While you hold your breath, the oxygen in your blood slowly *runs down*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So your body switches on its dive reflex: your heart slows, and blood leaves your hands and *feet*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then your spleen, a small organ under your ribs, squeezes like a *sponge*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It pushes spare red blood cells, which carry oxygen, into your blood like a *backup tank*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Seals have enormous spleens for exactly this *reason*.

shots.words: While you hold your breath, the oxygen in your blood slowly *runs down*.
So your body switches on its dive reflex: your heart slows, and blood leaves your hands and *feet*.
Then your spleen, a small organ under your ribs, squeezes like a *sponge*.
It pushes spare red blood cells, which carry oxygen, into your blood like a *backup tank*.
Seals have enormous spleens for exactly this *reason*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And here is the catch: the Bajau, sea nomads of Southeast Asia, have already grown a *bigger* tank.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Their divers spend up to sixty percent of a working day diving for *fish*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Scientists scanned the spleens of the Bajau and of their farming neighbours, the *Saluan*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The Bajau spleen was about fifty percent *bigger*, roughly the size of a tennis ball.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It was big even in Bajau who do not dive, so it is in their *genes*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Scientists think it took only around a thousand years at sea, a *blink* for evolution.

shots.words: And here is the catch: the Bajau, sea nomads of Southeast Asia, have already grown a *bigger* tank.
Their divers spend up to sixty percent of a working day diving for *fish*.
Scientists scanned the spleens of the Bajau and of their farming neighbours, the *Saluan*.
The Bajau spleen was about fifty percent *bigger*, roughly the size of a tennis ball.
It was big even in Bajau who do not dive, so it is in their *genes*.
Scientists think it took only around a thousand years at sea, a *blink* for evolution.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Melissa Ilardo's team published this in the journal *Cell* in 2018.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: They also found a gene, PDE10A, that may make the spleen *bigger*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Scientists think it works through a body hormone, but nobody has *proved* that yet.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The breath hold world record is twenty nine minutes, but only after breathing pure *oxygen*.

shots.words: Melissa Ilardo's team published this in the journal *Cell* in 2018.
They also found a gene, PDE10A, that may make the spleen *bigger*.
Scientists think it works through a body hormone, but nobody has *proved* that yet.
The breath hold world record is twenty nine minutes, but only after breathing pure *oxygen*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Next time you slip under the water, your heart is already *slowing* down.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your body is still running a diving program far *older* than you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So could humans evolve to hold their breath like seals? Slowly, yes, and one people is already *on the way*.
